title: The Extra Line on the Weekly Sheet
teaser: The weekly sheet had once cut driver waiting from forty-six minutes to nineteen, so no one had a reason to throw it away. The trouble began when a new client started adding orders in the afternoon: the team could see the new numbers, even add a new KPI, and still not know how to change the old way of working.
paragraphs: At 15:30 on Thursday, Lin Lan stood at the entrance to the packing area and looked at more than five hundred orders still waiting to be sealed. The last truck would arrive at 18:40, and she had to decide whether to open a second packing line. Three months earlier, afternoons like this often collapsed into disorder: materials went missing at the last minute, drivers queued outside, and overtime stretched into the evening. Then she put daily completion rate, picking errors, driver waiting, overtime hours, and packing-material shortages onto one weekly sheet, with focused intervention only when a measure moved outside its range. Six weeks later, average driver waiting had fallen from forty-six minutes to nineteen, and overtime was down by almost one-third. That day she followed the sheet and did not open another line. At 18:36, the last pallet was sealed.

In the autumn, the company began a trial with a fast-growing sports brand. This client behaved differently from the established ones: it launched products in the morning and added orders in the afternoon according to platform sales. Sales had accepted the pilot because the company explicitly wanted to serve growing brands of this kind. The warehouse also kept one safety line that could not be crossed: an unverified system interface could not write directly into inventory. For four weeks, the agreement was that additions made before 15:00, up to eighty orders a day, would still be checked against inventory manually. The first week passed without trouble, and the old measures on the weekly sheet remained normal.

At 14:45 in the second week, the client added seventy-six orders. The team leader saw the message but did not break open the main picking wave already in progress. Inserting the orders halfway through could raise picking errors and driver waiting, two service standards the warehouse had spent months stabilizing. He moved the additional orders to the next day. The same thing happened twice in the third week. For three weeks, the sheet showed four green measures and one yellow, while sales received four cancellation records. Three explicitly said, 'Moved to another warehouse for same-day handling.' No one had missed the messages, and the client had not exceeded the eighty-order limit. Every addition fell within the terms of the pilot.

Lin Lan tried the most direct fix first. She added 'same-day completion rate for additional orders' to the weekly sheet and set a target of 90 percent. The new measure changed attention immediately, but it did not create a stable way of working. The next time sixty-four orders arrived, the team inserted them into the main wave to protect the new target, and driver waiting rose to thirty-one minutes. The following day, another seventy-one orders came in. To avoid repeating the congestion, the supervisor pushed them to the next day. The old indicators turned green again; the new one turned yellow. Everyone was active in the group chat, and the weekly sheet now had one more line, but the same people were simply moving back and forth between two sets of targets.

From that week onward, Lin Lan blocked forty-five minutes every Wednesday afternoon and required each function to bring one issue that 'keeps recurring but cannot yet be explained by the current rules.' Sales brought the hourly order-growth curve. The packing supervisor brought records of workstation congestion from the two insertion attempts. IT pointed out that after 13:30 the system generated only one formal picking wave. The discussion did not touch the inventory interface and did not loosen the eighty-order cap. The team tested only one change: an independent small wave for additions received before 15:00, so they could be picked separately without breaking the main wave. When a similar addition arrived the following week, the team used the new method.

Four weeks later, same-day completion for added orders was 92 percent. Average driver waiting had risen from nineteen minutes to twenty-three, and for the first time the old weekly sheet showed two persistent yellow measures. At the same time, cancellations of added orders fell from four to zero. Only after manual inventory checks ran for four consecutive weeks without an error was the daily cap raised from eighty to one hundred and twenty. At year-end, when administration repainted the wall, someone asked whether the old sheet by the door should stay. Lin Lan pinned it back in the same place and hung a small whiteboard beside it. The latest row on the sheet read three green, two yellow. On the whiteboard she wrote only one question: What changed this week that this sheet alone can no longer answer?
concept: Simons' levers of control distinguish different control tasks. Diagnostic control works well for activities with clear targets and relatively stable relationships, using measures and deviations to support efficient execution. When new strategic uncertainties emerge, simply adding another measure may not be enough. Interactive control is needed to keep those changes in recurring management discussion and to alter assumptions, resource allocation, or working methods. Belief systems give direction to what the organization is willing to explore, while boundary systems define which actions remain off-limits even if they appear effective.
explanation: The story first shows that the old weekly sheet genuinely works for a mature warehouse process, so the problem is not that 'KPIs are harmful.' When the growing brand brings afternoon order additions, the team reasonably continues to protect picking accuracy, driver waiting, and the stability of the main wave. Sales, warehouse, and dispatch can all see the added orders, and Lin Lan even introduces a same-day completion target. The result is only oscillation between old and new indicators: one insertion creates congestion, and the next order is deferred again. This rules out the explanations that the team merely lacks data, communication, or one more KPI. The real behavioral turn comes after a recurring interactive discussion puts the order curve, workstation congestion, and system wave design together. That discussion changes the operating assumption that there can be only one main wave a day. The strategic intention to serve growing brands remains in place, and the safety boundary around the inventory interface and manual verification is never removed.
mapping: The original weekly sheet sharply reduces driver waiting and overtime → diagnostic control works in a stable, repetitive task and forms the normal baseline.

When afternoon additions appear, the team defers them to protect the main wave, picking accuracy, and driver waiting → existing diagnostic standards genuinely drive locally reasonable behavior while missing a new strategic uncertainty.

After 'same-day completion for additional orders' is added, one forced insertion creates congestion and the next order is deferred again → this rules out the idea that the problem is simply a missing KPI; the measure reveals the conflict but does not automatically generate a new operating assumption.

Recurring interactive discussion brings together order timing, workstation congestion, and system wave design, leading to an independent small wave while the inventory-interface boundary and manual checks remain → new information actually changes process and resource design, which is when interactive control begins to work.
boundary: Environmental change does not mean KPIs should be removed, and a recurring meeting is not automatically interactive control. Stable tasks still suit diagnostic control. An interactive mechanism exists only when strategic uncertainty is repeatedly brought into management discussion and actually changes assumptions, resource allocation, process design, or experiments. Strategic direction and boundary constraints must also shape real choices; otherwise they are only slogans or policy text.
reflection: If adding one more KPI only makes a team switch back and forth between two sets of targets, what kind of discussion would actually change what they do next time?
